title: Theo and the Autopsy
premise: Sebastian Quintana, the observant concierge of the Marlowe Hotel, has quietly unraveled three deaths the police ruled accidental — but her fourth case arrives as a confession letter postmarked one day after the victim's funeral, addressed to her by a name no one should know: the childhood name she buried when she left her old life behind. As she investigates, she realizes the killer is feeding her the case file piece by piece, someone who knows the investigators' mistakes intimately and is using her to expose a cover-up inside the police department. The trail leads to the autopsy of the victim — falsified by the one person Sebastian has come to love, Detective Ilya Marsh, who altered the report to protect his dying mentor's reputation and accidentally shielded a murderer. In the end, Sebastian must choose between handing Ilya to justice and using her knowledge of his falsification to trap the real killer, a forensic technician who has been quietly 'correcting' autopsies for years; she catches him with a staged confession letter of her own, and turns Ilya in, keeping only the letter — and the truth about herself — as her own.
about_author: Ansel Okafor is a former night-desk clerk at a historic coastal hotel who spent a decade collecting the strange, sad, and occasionally criminal stories guests leave behind at 3 a.m. He writes mysteries in which the people who watch — porters, cleaners, clerks — see everything the important people miss.

chapters.title: The Fourth Letter
chapters.summary: Sebastian Quintana, concierge of the Marlowe Hotel, receives an envelope postmarked the day after councilman Alden Voss's funeral, addressed to 'Ruthie' — a name she abandoned years ago. Inside is a confession to Voss's murder, written in careful, almost loving detail. Her POV. The beat is a cold drop of recognition: someone knows who she used to be.

chapters.title: Three Accidents, One Pattern
chapters.summary: Flashback woven into the present as Sebastian reviews her private notebook: three deaths she quietly solved while the police filed them as accidents. She never told anyone — except once, in a moment of weakness, she told Detective Ilya Marsh. Her POV. The beat is the uneasy pride of a woman who solves murders no one asked her to solve.

chapters.title: The Detective Who Listens
chapters.summary: Sebastian visits Ilya Marsh under the pretense of returning a guest's lost watch, testing how much he knows about the Voss case. He is distracted, defensive, and — she notices — wearing a black armband for a death no one announced. His POV briefly surfaces in dialogue. The beat is attraction sharpened into suspicion.

chapters.title: Autopsy 4417
chapters.summary: Sebastian pulls strings with a hospital archivist to see Voss's autopsy summary: cause of death listed as cardiac event, no mention of the bruising she saw on the body herself. Someone altered the record. Her POV. The beat is the first hard proof that the confession letter is telling the truth — and that the police are not.

chapters.title: The Killer Knows the File
chapters.summary: A second letter arrives, quoting the autopsy's internal case number and an investigator's typo — details never made public. Sebastian realizes her correspondent is either the killer or someone with full access to the file. Her POV. The beat is the vertigo of being outmaneuvered by someone who seems to be reading her moves before she makes them.

chapters.title: Ruthie
chapters.summary: Sebastian's carefully constructed identity begins to crack as she investigates who could know her childhood name: an old classmate, a family enemy, or the sister she hasn't spoken to in fifteen years. Her POV, with memory fragments of the night she left home. The beat is grief surfacing under the mystery.

chapters.title: The Widow's Lobby
chapters.summary: At the Marlowe, Sebastian works the Voss funeral reception, reading the widow, the business partner, and a nervous forensic technician named Corin Vale who asks oddly specific questions about hotel security cameras. Her POV. The beat is the pleasure of her craft — watching people who think no one is watching.

chapters.title: What Ilya Buried
chapters.summary: Sebastian tails Ilya to a cemetery where he visits the fresh grave of Dr. Halvorsen, the retired chief medical examiner. Ilya catches her watching. Neither lies well. His POV. The beat is two people who trust no one deciding, dangerously, to trust each other a little.

chapters.title: The Mentor's Signature
chapters.summary: Ilya admits Halvorsen signed Autopsy 4417 on the day he died — an impossible date. He altered the record to hide that his mentor's signature had been forged, fearing a scandal would exhume every case Halvorsen ever touched. Sebastian realizes his cover-up may be shielding the killer. Alternating POV. The beat is love and duty colliding in a hospital parking garage.

chapters.title: A Third Letter, Addressed to Ilya
chapters.summary: The correspondent writes to Ilya now, quoting his falsification verbatim — a threat. Sebastian and Ilya compare letters and realize the writer is orchestrating them both, steering their investigation. Her POV. The beat is the horror of realizing you are not the hunter but the instrument.

chapters.title: The Technician's Hours
chapters.summary: Sebastian cross-references Corin Vale's shifts with all four deaths — including her own three cold cases — and finds him present at every autopsy, every time. But the evidence is circumstantial, and Vale is beloved, meticulous, invisible. Her POV. The beat is the frustration of truth without proof.

chapters.title: The Sister Who Wrote
chapters.summary: Sebastian finally calls her estranged sister, Dana, and learns the name 'Ruthie' came from letters Dana wrote years ago — letters that were never delivered but were returned to sender, to an address someone else controlled. Her POV. The beat is an old wound reopened: someone has been collecting her past.

chapters.title: Dead Drop at the Marlowe
chapters.summary: The killer requests a meeting through a fourth letter: room 907, midnight, bring the autopsy discrepancy and come alone. Sebastian prepares — recording devices, an exit route, a lie to Ilya. Her POV. The beat is fear worn like a uniform, and the guilt of the lie.

chapters.title: Room 907
chapters.summary: The meeting is a trap of a different kind: the room is empty except for a tape recorder and a full copy of the Voss case file, annotated in the killer's hand — including a page Sebastian has never seen, one that names Ilya's falsification and her own old identity. Her POV. The beat is being known completely by a stranger.

chapters.title: The Confession That Wasn't
chapters.summary: Sebastian replays the recorder's message: Vale confesses in a flat, rehearsed voice — then the recording cuts to a second voice explaining that Vale is a scapegoat, that the real falsifications run deeper, and that the writer will kill again unless the file goes public. Her POV. The beat is the ground shifting: the confession letter was never a confession.

chapters.title: Two Liars, One Truth
chapters.summary: Sebastian and Ilya finally lay everything on the table — her identity, her three solved cases, his falsified report — and realize the killer's goal is not to hide the murders but to force the department to exhume Halvorsen's entire caseload, destroying the legacy Ilya is protecting. His POV. The beat is intimacy built from mutual confession, and the terrible clarity it brings.

chapters.title: The Fifth Death
chapters.summary: Corin Vale is found dead in the hospital morgue, staged to look like suicide, with a final letter naming Ilya as the falsifier — the frame closing. Sebastian spots the one detail that's wrong: the letter's postmark predates Vale's death. Her POV. The beat is grief and fury fused into resolve.

chapters.title: The Hand That Signs
chapters.summary: Sebastian traces the forged signature technique — a fluid, confident hand — to Acting Medical Examiner Dr. Yusra Bedri, Halvorsen's protégée, who has been 'correcting' inconvenient autopsies for a decade and killing the few who noticed. The letters were her insurance policy against Ilya. Her POV. The beat is the cold satisfaction of the pattern finally closing.

chapters.title: Bait in the File Room
chapters.summary: Sebastian plants a forged letter of her own — quoting Bedri's private phrases, postmarked tomorrow, addressed to the press — and lets it be found in the case file room. Ilya, against duty and career, backs her play by pulling Bedri's old cases for review. Alternating POV. The beat is love against duty, both of them choosing the trap over safety.

chapters.title: The Last Autopsy
chapters.summary: Bedri takes the bait and comes for Sebastian at the Marlowe, intending one more 'accidental' death. In the hotel's back corridors Sebastian turns the killer's own method against her — observation, patience, a recorded confession drawn out by flattery and fear — while Ilya and the police close in. Her POV. The beat is the climax: the watcher watched, and the watcher wins.

chapters.title: What the Report Says
chapters.summary: In the aftermath, Sebastian must decide what to do with the evidence of Ilya's falsification. She gives the state everything except the page bearing her old name, and testifies to the truth of his crime — and his motive. Ilya is suspended, facing charges, and does not hate her for it. Her POV. The beat is duty honored at the cost of love, and the strange peace of having chosen correctly.

chapters.title: Concierge, Desk One
chapters.summary: Months later, Sebastian returns to the Marlowe desk, her notebook heavier, her name — both of them — finally her own. Ilya appears as a guest, no longer a detective, and asks for a room; she gives him one, and a dinner invitation, and nothing forgiven that shouldn't be. Her POV, closing the frame with a new letter on the desk she chooses not to open yet. The beat is quiet resolution: identity survived, loyalty redefined, truth kept.
